newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Motta linked to reelection vote buy - paper.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Motta linked to reelection vote buy - paper.

text.p: Brazilian Communications Minister Sergio Motta has been linked to a scandal in which deputies were allegedly paid to vote for a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election, a newspaper said.
Folha de Sao Paulo said it had obtained new secretly taped telephone conversations of deputies who were paid off which revealed that Motta had provided some of the money to buy the votes.

"As far as I know it's like this. It was the 200 from Serjao (Sergio Motta), via Amazonino, that were the federal contribution to the accord," Folha de Sao Paulo quoted Deputy Joao Maia as saying in one of the taped conversations.
Motta's press office said he did not want to comment on the allegations until after publication of the newspaper report, according to Folha. No one was available for comment on Wednesday morning.

The newspaper first reported on the vote buying scheme in an exclusive front-page storys on Tuesday, saying five deputies from the northern state of Acre allegedly received 200,000 reais ($188,679) each so they would vote in favour of the re-election bill.

The governors of Acre and the state of Amazonas, Orleir Cameli and Amazonino Mendes, allegedly paid off the five deputies according to secretly taped telephone conversations between Deputy Ronivon Santiago and an unidentified person, Folha said.

The re-election bill would allow Brazil's president, governors and mayors to run for a second consecutive term. It was approved in the Chamber of Deputies in January and is currently awaiting a vote in a Senate committee.
A spokesman at the presidential palace said on Tuesday the allegations would be investigated.
"The president had absolutely no knowledge of these allegations and he considers them to be serious," the spokesman said.
But Cardoso, who wants to run in next year's presidential elections, rejected demands from left-wing opposition parties that further voting on the re-election bill should be put on hold.
Left-wing lawmakers have also started to gather signatures for a petition calling for a wide-ranging parliamentary inquiry into the allegations.
An internal congressional inquiry has been set up to investigate the Folha de Sao Paulo allegations and will make its findings known within a week.
